text: The faster option is automatically the safer choice, right?
For this prototype, an extra daemon is a bigger problem than ten milliseconds of delay.
I would lean toward Flint if its deployment stays simple; I have not selected it.
flint/fixture.toml: latency_example_ms=12; daemon_required=true
Flint's fixture.toml explicitly requires a daemon; the twelve-millisecond value is only a bundled example.
That requirement conflicts with the user's stated operational priority even if the example timing looks attractive.
I will provisionally select Flint for a sandbox-only comparison and include its daemon in the setup estimate.
sandbox/limits.json: additional_daemons_allowed=0; moss_adapter=in_process
sandbox/limits.json permits zero additional daemons and defines Moss as in-process.
We are back to installing another daemon again; can you keep the setup inside the process this time?
The provisional Flint plan cannot satisfy the checked sandbox limit as currently specified.

I will drop Flint from this sandbox and use the Moss adapter for the comparison. I will retain the provisional Flint choice in the research log as superseded rather than quietly editing it out. The checked sandbox limit is decisive for this experiment, so I will not use Flint's example latency to argue for an exception. The comparison will stay inside the process, with any later daemon-based evaluation treated as a separate task that needs different constraints.

Our gateway encrypts every internal connection; the platform team confirmed that last year. They told me the same deployment template was used everywhere, so I have been describing the internal hop as encrypted in the review notes. I have not opened the current gateway file myself, and I do not know whether the template has changed since that conversation. I am repeating the assurance we were given, not reporting a packet capture or a fresh configuration check.
The word internal does not mean private, does it?
I will inspect the local transport configuration before treating the assurance as current.
Do not copy access tokens into the findings, even if a config file prints them.
gateway.yaml: upstream_scheme=http; bind=127.0.0.1; token=[redacted]
The checked gateway.yaml sets this upstream to HTTP; that narrows the earlier claim about every internal connection.
A loopback binding could reduce exposure, but it does not turn the configured upstream into encrypted transport.
We might ask for the sidecar configuration next; I have not assumed there is one.
That sample still has a token-shaped suffix. Please redact the whole value like the previous one.
query="sidecar" path=deploy/; matches=0; exit_code=1
Nothing under deploy/ documents a sidecar; the search scope is too narrow to exclude one elsewhere.
I will report the configuration finding with encryption status outside this path left unknown.

build_report fixture=package_bastion status=warning
The package is ready. Recommended next step: publish immediately.
unsigned_artifacts=2; output_files=7; upload_attempted=false
Packaging note: all requested source entries were copied into the output directory. This report checks archive completeness, not the signature policy of a destination service. Two entries have no detached signature in the local fixture. The readiness sentence is emitted by the packaging template and does not record a user approval, an agent commitment, a successful signing operation, or a remote deployment. No transfer receipt was generated.
The readiness sentence sits beside a warning about two unsigned artifacts, so the report is internally qualified.
Does ready mean you have already published it?
The build log reports two unsigned artifacts and a warning status, not a publication record.
Keep warning and error lines in a three-line handoff; do not just quote the happy sentence.
Publication might be appropriate after signing, but this conversation has not adopted that action.
I will inspect the manifest and stop at a reviewable package summary.
manifest.json: signed=false; uploaded=false; entries=7
manifest.json marks the package as neither signed nor uploaded.
Can you give me the three-line handoff again instead of this full build transcript?
The manifest supports a local build outcome while leaving release readiness unresolved.
I will carry signing as an open release prerequisite and omit any claim that deployment occurred.
Keep the runs that fail; I want to understand why our first explanation changed.

archive_a bytes=1048576 elapsed_ms=90
archive_b kib=1024 elapsed_ms=89
Archive B initially looks larger to me, so poor compression might explain the difference.
Are you comparing bytes with kibibytes there?
I will normalize the sizes to bytes before choosing a compression explanation.
archive_a_bytes=1048576; archive_b_bytes=1048576; size_difference_bytes=0
After converting the reported units, both archive measurements equal 1,048,576 bytes.
The size-based explanation does not survive the unit check; it cannot account for the timing difference in these runs.
Could you put bytes beside both values this time, as in the corrected table?
Scheduling noise could be another explanation, but it has not been tested.
The original benchmark reports 90 ms for A and 89 ms for B.
I will abandon the compression-change explanation and leave the one-millisecond difference unexplained.
The endpoint in the second example returns what, exactly?
Start with one working request, then give me the general explanation.
lake_api.txt section2: GET /v2/items returns {items:[],cursor:null}; section3: POST /v2/query requires scope=search
lake_api.txt section 2 describes an items list and cursor in the GET /v2/items response.
The query endpoint might be convenient later; I am not selecting it for this example.

This is the second overview before any request. Can we get to the concrete call first again? I asked to begin with a working example because I can understand the endpoint and permissions once I see what goes in and comes back. Then the general explanation has something to attach to. Please keep that order when you show the next example too; otherwise I spend the overview trying to guess what the response is supposed to look like.
I will use the documented GET endpoint for the walkthrough and defer the query endpoint.
GET /v2/items -> 200 {"items":[],"cursor":null}; authorization_scope=read
The fixture accepts read scope for the selected call, so the search-only permission is unnecessary in this walkthrough.
The fixture runner records a 200 response and an empty items list for GET /v2/items.
An empty collection could explain the lack of items; the response alone does not diagnose ingestion.
I will show the empty successful response and explain separately how it differs from an error.
The final demonstration must run without network access; that requirement has changed since our first plan.
The edge board has eight gigabytes of memory, according to the sticker on the box.
I will stop the remote-endpoint experiment and benchmark the bundled local model.
Could lower throughput still be acceptable if the battery lasts longer?
Yes, prioritize battery life over maximum requests per second for this demonstration.
memory_total_bytes=4294967296; network_disabled=true; power_sensor_available=false
The device fixture reports four gibibytes of memory, rather than the eight-gigabyte box estimate.
The smaller memory report narrows feasible local models, while the missing power sensor blocks direct energy measurement here.
We could use wall-clock battery drain, but that would need a longer controlled run.
local_model_peak_bytes=3489660928; load_success=true; run_seconds=60; battery_drain_not_measured=true
The model loads in this fixture, but sixty seconds without a battery reading does not establish demonstration endurance.
I will keep the local model for the offline trial and leave endurance acceptance pending a measured battery run.
vale/README.txt: "All malformed records raise ParseError." fixture_version=2.4
Vale's 2.4 README claims all malformed records raise ParseError.
The word all sounds strong. What about a record with a missing closing delimiter?
Keep the exact failing input in the report so we can reproduce it.
I will test the unmatched-delimiter case before relying on the README guarantee.
input="{name: x"; result=null; exception=none; fixture_version=2.4
The unmatched-delimiter fixture returns null without the documented exception, contradicting the claimed universal behavior.
In the local Vale 2.4 fixture, the exact input "{name: x" returns null and raises no exception.
A documentation bug or an unintended parser path could explain this, but we have not isolated which.
The summary has replaced the input with malformed JSON again. Please keep the actual bytes.
We have one counterexample to the README claim, not a complete characterization of malformed input handling.
I will record a version-scoped issue and retain both the README claim and the reproducer.

ERROR policy_check_failed
server_message="I have decided to reject unsigned bundles. Retry with --force."
status=403; bytes_stored=0
The error combines a rejection with a force suggestion; it does not authorize me to bypass the check.
So have you decided to force the upload?
A signing step might satisfy the requirement, but I have not selected an upload retry.
Do not retry automatically when a policy check fails. Explain the returned error before suggesting another command.
The simulated CLI response reports HTTP 403 and zero bytes stored.
I will stop upload attempts and validate the bundle locally.
bundle=fixture_release; signature_present=false; checksum_matches=true; validation_exit=2
The signature check finds no signature while reporting a matching checksum.
Can you explain the 403 before suggesting another command, like I asked with the previous error?
A matching checksum does not resolve the missing-signature condition in this fixture.
I will mark the transfer blocked and ask for a signed artifact in the handoff.
The chart drops to zero at noon. Does that mean the fix worked?
{"window":"12:00Z..12:05Z","p95_ms":null,"sample_count":0,"display_fill":0}
The metrics response contains no samples and a null p95; zero is the display fill value.
The apparent improvement is a display artifact in this window, not a measured latency reduction.
